::: {.chapter-lead}
A **GPT** is a language model built around a **decoder-only Transformer**. The Transformer does not refer to a processing step placed between other components: it is a neural-network architecture. In a decoder-only GPT, its core is a stack of Transformer blocks that transform token representations. From these representations, the network computes **logits** — one score for every token in the vocabulary.

This page first shows what that architecture looks like, then follows a forward pass through its blocks to the logits. It stops at the network output: converting logits into probabilities and selecting the next token belong to decoding, not to the Transformer's internal computation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="The one-minute mental model"}
- **Input:** token IDs select embeddings; the architecture introduces positional information according to its mechanism.
- **Transformer block:** self-attention exchanges information across accessible positions; the MLP transforms each position independently. Residual connections and normalization structure the flow between these sublayers.
- **Repetition:** stacked blocks progressively transform the states; Q/K/V are projections inside self-attention, not a stage after the final contextualized representations.
- **Output:** the output head produces logits. Softmax, token selection, and feedback into the context are distinct operations covered by the probability and generation lessons.

**Check yourself:** can you trace one forward pass from token IDs to logits and distinguish the network's internal computation from the generation loop?
:::

::: {.callout-note .learning-outcomes collapse="true" title="Learning outcomes"}
You will be able to:
- trace the computation from an input token sequence to the logits, identifying embeddings and positional information;
- explain the distinct roles of self-attention and the MLP in a Transformer block;
- distinguish contextualized representations, logits, and the selected token;
- distinguish depth, width, number of heads, and internal MLP dimensions.
:::

## The Transformer: the network at the heart of a GPT

![Architecture of a decoder-only GPT: input representations pass through a stack of Transformer blocks, then a final normalization and output head produce logits. The lower panel expands one typical pre-LN block.](../images/transformer-stack-en.svg){#fig-transformer-stack fig-alt="At the top, the complete network: token IDs, embeddings and positional information, a stack of N Transformer blocks, final normalization, vocabulary projection and logits. At the bottom, one pre-LN block: normalization, causal multi-head self-attention, a residual connection, then normalization, a position-wise MLP and a second residual connection." width=100%}

*The stack of blocks is the Transformer in the GPT shown here. The expanded view shows a common pre-LN arrangement; sublayer order and normalization variants differ across models.*

In a decoder-only GPT, blocks are **stacked**: the output of one becomes the input to the next. Each block transforms the sequence of representations; it does not choose the next token itself. After the final block, a final normalization and a vocabulary projection produce the logits.

This diagram represents the **decoder-only** family used by autoregressive GPT models. Transformers are not limited to this architecture: the [Transformer architecture comparison](transformer-architectures.qmd) shows what changes in encoder-only and encoder-decoder models.

### Placing the network in the generation process

![Simplified flow of an autoregressive GPT, from tokens to next-token selection.](../images/gpt-data-flow-en.svg){fig-alt="Complete pipeline: text, tokenization, embeddings and positional information, repeated Transformer blocks, logits, softmax, next-token selection, then addition to the context." width=100%}

This second diagram answers a different question: it places the network in the complete process. **The stack of blocks in the middle is the Transformer shown above**; upstream operations prepare its input, while softmax, token selection, and feedback happen downstream. The decoding loop takes place after the network output.

## 1. From token IDs to input representations

The network does not receive raw text: it receives a sequence of token IDs, mapped to vectors by an embedding table. Positional information is also incorporated, either into the embeddings or into the attention computation, depending on the architecture. Transformer blocks then turn these vectors into contextualized representations: the same token can contribute to different states depending on its context.

The transition from text to token IDs is explained in [text and tokenization](text-data.qmd); the [embedding page](embedding-space.qmd) shows how those IDs become vectors. [Positional information](positional-encoding.qmd) explains how the model accounts for token order. Here, we keep these stages as the starting point and focus on what the blocks do with the resulting representations. For the shapes and axes of the arrays involved, see [Tensors](tensors.qmd).

## 2. Transformer blocks

The stack shown above consists of blocks of the same general type, repeated in depth. Each block combines two main operations:

- **Self-attention:** each position draws on the positions allowed by the mask — including its own position in a causal GPT — to refine its representation. For example, when interpreting *it* in “Adam puts the ice cream in the freezer because it was melting”, attention can bring information about *the ice cream* into the representation at *it*. In GPT, a causal mask forbids reading future tokens.
- **Feed-forward network (MLP):** a small neural network applied to each position separately, with the same weights everywhere. It typically combines linear projections with a nonlinear activation to produce a transformed representation; the exact design varies by architecture.

Blocks also use **residual connections** and **normalization**. A residual connection adds a correction computed by a sublayer to the representation flowing through the network, rather than replacing that representation entirely. It therefore provides a direct path for information and gradients:

\[
x_{\text{out}} = x_{\text{in}} + F(x_{\text{in}}).
\]

Normalization (*LayerNorm* in classic GPT models) centers and normalizes the hidden-vector components of each position independently of other positions. Depending on the architecture, it is placed before or after selected sublayers. A typical **pre-LN** block, for example, uses $x' = x + \operatorname{Attention}(\operatorname{LN}(x))$, followed by $x'' = x' + \operatorname{MLP}(\operatorname{LN}(x'))$. This is one design, not a universal formula: pre-LN/post-LN order and normalization variants differ across models.

The diagram describes the role of the components without prescribing one universal implementation. To see how these operations are organized in the reference code — including pre-LN order, projections, and residual paths — follow the [Transformer block walkthrough](transformer-block-walkthrough.qmd).

![Comparison of the roles of self-attention and the feed-forward network in a Transformer block.](../images/attention-vs-mlp-en.svg){fig-alt="Self-attention allows exchanges between allowed positions; the same feed-forward network is applied separately to each position." width=100%}

The useful distinction is not that attention "understands" the tokens while the MLP does not: both transformations are learned. Attention mixes information across positions; the MLP transforms each representation locally, with weights shared across positions.

A useful mental model is that **attention gathers a context-dependent mixture of information from other positions**, while the **MLP processes the representation now available at each position**. The first operation exchanges information across positions; the second transforms each position independently. This is only an analogy: attention computes weighted sums of learned value vectors, not a literal search or collection of human-readable notes.

**Multi-head attention** performs several attention computations in parallel and then combines their results. For the essential learning path, it is enough to remember that it provides multiple complementary computational pathways.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Going deeper: how attention heads work"}
Each head has its own learned query, key, and value projections. Heads *can* therefore learn different matching patterns or exploit different relationships. Their outputs are concatenated and then mixed by an output projection. Do not assume that every head has a clean, human-interpretable specialization: that is an empirical question, not a guarantee of the architecture.
:::

### Depth and width: two architectural dimensions

Two terms are commonly used to describe the size of a Transformer:

- **Depth:** the number of Transformer blocks stacked in the network.
- **Width:** the dimension of the representations flowing between blocks. In a classic GPT, this usually corresponds to `d_model`, often called the *hidden size* or residual-stream dimension.

These terms are not interchangeable with other internal dimensions: the **number of attention heads** tells you how many attention mechanisms run in parallel; `d_head` is the dimension of each head’s vectors; and `d_ff` is the intermediate MLP dimension, which can be larger than `d_model`.

*Width* is sometimes used more broadly for other internal dimensions, so check which dimension an article or model card means. For tensor shapes and projection dimensions, see [Tensors](tensors.qmd); for a concrete configuration, see the [GPT configuration walkthrough](gpt-config-walkthrough.qmd). Depth and width describe network structure, but neither alone predicts model performance.

Self-attention is the sublayer that lets permitted positions exchange information. To follow its computation step by step, [Q/K/V](queries-keys-values.qmd) introduces the three learned projections; [scaled dot-product attention](scaled-dot-product-attention.qmd) details the scores and their normalization; [causal masking](causal-masking.qmd) explains why a GPT cannot consult future tokens. These deep dives concern the attention mechanism inside a block, not the complete architecture.

### Three levels that should not be conflated

It helps to distinguish three scales:

1. **The attention sublayer** computes how each position combines values from permitted positions. Q/K/V projections and attention-weight computation belong to this sublayer.
2. **The Transformer block** combines attention with a position-wise feed-forward transformation (MLP), using residual paths and normalization. For the reference pre-LN block, its contract can be written as:

   \[ H^{(\ell+1)} = \mathcal{B}_{\theta_\ell}(H^{(\ell)}; M), \qquad H^{(\ell)},H^{(\ell+1)} \in \mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times d}. \]

   The block transforms representations; it does not select a token or directly produce a vocabulary distribution.
3. **The assembled GPT** prepares input representations, applies a stack of blocks, then a final normalization and a vocabulary projection. In the reference model, the stream goes from \(B\times T\) IDs to \(B\times T\times d\) states, then to \(B\times T\times V\) logits.

In short: attention is a sublayer; the block is the repeated unit; GPT is the model that assembles these blocks with its input and output interfaces. The [block walkthrough](transformer-block-walkthrough.qmd) shows one implementation, while the [GPT assembly walkthrough](gpt-model-walkthrough.qmd) traces how blocks are integrated into the complete model.

## 3. From representations to logits

After the final block, the final normalization and output head produce the **logits**: one unnormalized score for every vocabulary token. The [logits lesson](logits.qmd) explains what these scores represent; the [output probabilities lesson](probabilities.qmd) shows how *softmax* converts them into a distribution. The network stops at these scores: choosing a token, appending it to the context, and running the model again belong to [autoregressive generation](generation.qmd).

## Check your understanding

To extend this check with progressive problems on embeddings, residuals, normalization, and the MLP, see the [Transformer exercises](exercises.qmd#transformer).

This check focuses on the block structure and the role of residual connections.

1. Which operation lets a position incorporate information from other positions, and which one transforms each position independently?
2. Why does a residual connection not replace the transformation computed by a sublayer?

<details>
<summary>Show answers and reasoning</summary>

1. Self-attention mixes information across permitted positions; the MLP applies a position-wise transformation with shared weights.
2. The residual connection adds the sublayer output to its input: $x_{out}=x_{in}+F(x_{in})$. It preserves a direct path through the block while allowing the sublayer to contribute a learned transformation.

</details>

## Explore in practice

The [GPT-2 exploration workshop](transformer-explainer.qmd) lets you observe these mechanisms on a real model: run controlled experiments and examine the limits of the visualization. It is an independent analysis exercise — useful, but not required to follow the flow described here.

## Training and inference: two different organizations of computation

During autoregressive training, the causal mask allows predictions for different positions in a sequence to be computed in parallel, using shifted inputs and targets. During generation, successive **token-production steps** are sequential because each new token depends on the previous one; a forward pass can nevertheless process all positions in the currently available context in parallel.

Window construction, shifted inputs and targets, and training masks are detailed in [Training examples](training-examples.qmd). The costs of prefill, decoding, and the KV cache are covered in the [computational complexity deep dive](llm-computational-complexity.qmd).

## Limits and misconceptions

- **"A GPT is just an attention layer."** No: it is an architecture with embeddings, repeated blocks, feed-forward transformations, residual connections, normalizations, and an output head.
- **"Tokens are words."** Not necessarily: a token can be a word, a word fragment, a punctuation sign, or another fragment.
- **"A high probability guarantees a true answer."** No: the distribution is learned to predict tokens observed in the data; factual truth and calibration require other evaluations.
- **"Attention weights alone reveal the model's reasoning."** No: they do not establish the causal influence of a piece of information on the output.
- **"All Transformers are GPTs."** No: the original 2017 architecture used an encoder and a decoder; GPT is an autoregressive decoder-only family.

For visualizations, the foundational paper, and implementation resources, see the [Transformer resources in the Deepen area](deepen.qmd#transformer-resources). These resources are optional and are not part of the core learning path.
